description: We are a passionate team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are interested in space technology, Python, AI/ML and problem-solving. We enjoy learning new technologies and building creative solutions to real-world challenges. We are looking for enthusiastic and dedicated teammates with skills in Python, AI/ML, software development, UI/UX or space science who are ready to collaborate, learn and create something impactful!
summary:
Red Planet Rescue is an interactive Mars outpost survival simulator built for the challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”. Students act as Mission Commander and run an outpost of six astronauts for 30 Martian days (sols), balancing oxygen, water, food and power against Martian weather.

It addresses the challenge by making engineering trade-offs tangible. Every decision has a cost: rationing water adds supply but raises crew stress, and the emergency oxygen generator saves air but drains the battery. Dust storms cut solar power, and a cascade failure map shows how one problem spreads to others, such as a storm leading to a water shortage. Four rule-based advisors (Chief Engineer, Medical Officer, Mission Commander, Risk Analyst) explain their recommendations and risk levels, so players learn why, not just what. Crew, Explore and Mission Report pages track astronaut health, explain real Martian conditions and score the final outcome.

It matters because young learners often meet space engineering as oversimplified or too complex. This simulator lets them experience why missions succeed or fail by making the decisions themselves.
details:
Challenge
Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

1. What it does and how it works
Red Planet Rescue is a web-based Mars outpost survival simulator. The player takes the role of Mission Commander and manages six astronauts for 30 Martian days (sols). Four critical resources are tracked: oxygen, water, food and battery power. Each sol, these resources decrease according to crew consumption and Martian weather, which ranges from normal conditions to a severe dust storm that cuts solar output to 15%. The player makes one decision per sol from six options, such as rationing water, repairing solar panels or giving the crew a rest day. Every option improves one area and has a cost in another. A cascade failure map shows how one event spreads: a dust storm lowers solar power, the battery drains, water recycling slows and the risk of a water shortage rises. Four rule-based advisors (Chief Engineer, Medical Officer, Mission Commander and Risk Analyst) give recommendations with reasons and risk levels. At the end of the mission, a report presents the survival rate, score, grade and a timeline of key events.

2. Benefits
The simulator makes engineering trade-offs tangible for young learners. Students see cause and effect directly, and because every advisor explains its reasoning, they learn why a decision is made and not only what to choose. It runs in a standard web browser on laptops and phones, so no installation or special hardware is needed.

3. Intended impact
Space-themed STEM content is often oversimplified or too complex for young learners. Our aim is for students to finish a mission understanding why real missions succeed or fail, because they experienced the consequences of their own decisions. The weather schedule is fixed, so every run is repeatable and a class can compare strategies and discuss which choices worked best.

4. Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, Vite, JavaScript, HTML and CSS
  • Backend and data: Python Flask with a REST API (JSON)
  • Development: Git, GitHub and Visual Studio Code
  • Hardware: standard laptops, no special equipment

5. How the project is creative
Our cascade failure map explains each step of a failure with a stated reason, which turns the game into a reasoning exercise. Crew health, fatigue, stress and morale respond to supplies, weather and the player’s choices, so decisions have human consequences. A resource forecast shows when each supply would run out if nothing changes, which encourages planning ahead. An Explore page links seven real Martian conditions, such as thin atmosphere, extreme cold, low gravity and communication delay, to the rules of the game.

6. Factors our team considered
We designed rules simple enough for young learners yet realistic enough to teach genuine trade-offs. We kept the advisors rule-based so every recommendation can be traced to a clear reason. We built a working simulator first and added visual features afterwards, and we made the layout responsive for laptop, tablet and phone screens.
